question.text:
You are a portfolio manager provided with the expected return and standard deviation of four assets. Asset A: Expected Mean Return: 5%, Standard Deviation: 0; Asset B: Expected Mean Return: 10%, Standard Deviation: 10%; Asset C: Expected Mean Return: 12%, Standard Deviation: 15%; Asset D: Expected Mean Return: 7%, Standard Deviation: 17%.
If you could invest in only one of the three assets (A, B, or C), which one would you pick?

answer.text: Any of them depending upon the risk profile of the investor and investment objectives

explanation.text: The Logic: Without knowing the investor's risk profile or objective, no single asset can be picked as universally best among A, B and C. Asset C offers the highest expected return (12%) for an aggressive investor, Asset A has zero standard deviation for a risk-averse investor, and Asset B (10% return, 10% SD) sits in the middle. Hence the answer is profile-dependent. The Trap: 'A' tempts because zero SD feels 'safe', 'C' tempts because 12% is the highest number on the page, and 'B' tempts as the balanced middle choice. Each is right only for a specific risk profile; selecting one without the client's risk tolerance is the classic 'product-push' trap rather than goals-based advice. Cross-Exam Context: Same risk-profiling and efficient-frontier logic surfaces in NISM-Series-X-A (Investment Adviser Level 1), X-B (Level 2) and XXI-B (PMS Investment Adviser). Distributor's Pro-Tip: In the first client meeting, anchor the product pitch to a written risk profile and investment policy statement — never recommend an asset purely on headline return, because the compliance trail in a PMS client agreement demands a documented suitability link.
